questions.question: (TCP three-way handshake time-line diagram given.) 1. Identify which host is the client and which is the server. 2. Fill in the missing acknowledgment number in the second segment and the sequence number and flag of the third segment.
questions.solution:
1. Left side (active open) -> Client; the host that performs active open sends the first SYN. Right side (passive open) -> Server; the host that performs passive open waits for a connection and replies with SYN + ACK.
2. First segment: client -> server, seq = 8000, SYN flag set (no ACK since it is the first packet). Second segment: server -> client, seq = 15000, SYN + ACK set; it must acknowledge the client's SYN, so ACK = 8000 + 1 = 8001. Third segment: client -> server, acknowledges the server's SYN, ack = 15000 + 1 = 15001; usually no SYN flag now, only ACK; the sequence number continues from the previous one, seq = 8001. Third segment details: seq = 8001, ack = 15001, Flag: ACK.
questions.breakdown_text: 2+3 (2M for the identification, 3M for the segment fields)

rubric.point: The host performing the active open (left) is the client and sends the first SYN; the host performing the passive open (right) is the server and replies SYN+ACK
Second segment acknowledgment number = 8000 + 1 = 8001
Third segment sequence number seq = 8001 and ack = 15000 + 1 = 15001
Third segment carries the ACK flag only, with no SYN

questions.question: In a TCP session, two consecutive segments are sent and acknowledged by a single cumulative ACK, which is later lost. If no further data is sent, answer the following: 1. What event triggers retransmission at the sender? 2. Which segment is retransmitted? 3. What does the receiver do upon receiving this duplicate segment? 4. How does the sender confirm that both original segments were successfully received? 5. Explain why only one segment is retransmitted even though two segments remain unacknowledged after the ACK loss.
questions.solution:
1. Since no more data is being sent, no further ACKs arrive and no duplicate ACKs can be generated. Therefore the retransmission timer (RTO) at the sender expires.
2. When the RTO expires the sender retransmits the oldest unacknowledged segment - the one starting with sequence number 501. Retransmitted segment: Seq = 501-600.
3. The receiver has already received and acknowledged all data up to 700. When it receives Seq = 501-600 again it recognises a duplicate segment, discards the duplicate data, and resends the same cumulative ACK = 701.
4. When the sender receives ACK = 701 it knows all bytes up to 700 - both segments 501-600 and 601-700 - were successfully received.
5. Even though both segments appear unacknowledged, TCP's retransmission rule states that after an RTO only the earliest unacknowledged segment is retransmitted. Once it is resent the receiver responds with cumulative ACK = 701, and TCP's cumulative ACKs mean a single ACK can acknowledge multiple segments.

rubric.point: The retransmission timer (RTO) expiring at the sender is what triggers retransmission, because no further or duplicate ACKs can arrive
The oldest unacknowledged segment is retransmitted - the one starting at sequence number 501, i.e. Seq = 501-600
The receiver recognises it as a duplicate, discards the duplicate data, and resends the same cumulative ACK = 701
Receiving ACK = 701 tells the sender that all bytes up to 700 arrived, confirming both original segments
After an RTO only the earliest unacknowledged segment is retransmitted; TCP's cumulative ACK then covers the rest

questions.question: For the network given in the figure, the routing tables of the four nodes A, E, D and G are shown. Suppose that F has estimated its delay to its neighbours A, E, D and G as 8, 10, 12 and 6 msec respectively, and updates its routing table using the distance vector routing technique. Provide the new updated routing table of node F using the data provided.
questions.solution:
Compute, for each destination, cost via each neighbour and take the minimum:
A: via A 8+0=8, via E 10+24=34, via D 12+20=32, via G 6+21=27 -> best 8 (A)
B: via A 8+40=48, via E 10+27=37, via D 12+8=20, via G 6+24=30 -> best 20 (D)
C: via A 8+14=22, via E 10+7=17, via D 12+30=42, via G 6+22=28 -> best 17 (E)
D: via A 8+17=25, via E 10+20=30, via D 12+0=12, via G 6+19=25 -> best 12 (D)
E: via A 8+21=29, via E 10+0=10, via D 12+14=26, via G 6+22=28 -> best 10 (E)
F: 0 (self)
G: via A 8+24=32, via E 10+22=32, via D 12+22=34, via G 6+0=6 -> best 6 (G)
Updated routing table of node F: A 8 via A; B 20 via D; C 17 via E; D 12 via D; E 10 via E; F 0; G 6 via G.
questions.breakdown_text: The scheme prints 5X1 but does not say which five things earn the five marks, and node F has six non-self destinations. The grouping below is ours.

rubric.point: Applies the distance vector rule: cost to a destination via a neighbour is the link cost to that neighbour plus the neighbour's advertised distance, and the minimum is taken
Destination A = 8 via A, and destination G = 6 via G (the direct links are the cheapest)
Destination B = 20 via D
Destination C = 17 via E
Destination D = 12 via D and destination E = 10 via E

notes: The answer is naturally a table. Expect many students to have drawn one, in which case the reading of this part arrives as a figure crop and the item goes to the human tier rather than being scored on prose.

NO `exact` VALUES ON THIS QUESTION, DELIBERATELY. The answers are 8, 20, 17, 12, 10, 6 - and every one of those numbers already appears in the routing tables the question hands the student. A tier-1 match would fire on a student who merely copied the given data, which is the opposite of evidence. The numbers stay in `keywords`, where they are one signal among several, and the item is allowed to go up the ladder.

questions.question: 1. In an IP packet the value of HLEN is 6 (hex) and the value of the total length field is 0038 (hex). How many bytes of data are being carried by this packet? 2. An IP packet of size 1600 bytes passes through a network segment before it reaches its destination. The header size of this packet is 30 bytes. The maximum size of an IP packet in an intermediate network (MTU) is 1400 bytes. How would the IP packet be fragmented in a router? Find all the information for each fragment.
questions.solution:
1. Each HLEN unit = 4 bytes, so header length = 6 x 4 = 24 bytes. Total length (0038)16 = 3 x 16 + 8 = 56. Data size = total length - header length = 56 - 24 = 32 bytes.
2. Data in the original packet = 1600 - 30 = 1570 bytes. Each fragment must include its own 30-byte header, so maximum data per fragment = 1400 - 30 = 1370 bytes. Fragment offsets are measured in units of 8 bytes, so each fragment's data size must be a multiple of 8: 1370 / 8 = 171.25, and the largest multiple of 8 below 1370 is 171 x 8 = 1368 bytes. Dividing 1570 into chunks of 1368: fragment 1 carries 1368 bytes, leaving 1570 - 1368 = 202 bytes. So there are 2 fragments - #1 with 1368 bytes of data and total size 1398, #2 with 202 bytes of data and total size 232. Both are <= MTU (1400).
Fragment 1: offset = 0, MF = 1, total length = 1398 bytes.
Fragment 2: offset = 1368 / 8 = 171, MF = 0, total length = 232 bytes.
questions.breakdown_text: 2+3 (2M for the HLEN/data-size calculation, 3M for the fragmentation)

rubric.point: Header = 6 x 4 = 24 bytes, total length 0038 hex = 56, so data = 56 - 24 = 32 bytes
Data in the original packet is 1600 - 30 = 1570 bytes, and the maximum data per fragment is 1400 - 30 = 1370, cut down to the multiple of 8 below it, 1368
Two fragments result: 1368 bytes of data (total size 1398) and 202 bytes of data (total size 232)
Fragment 1 has offset 0 with MF = 1; fragment 2 has offset 1368/8 = 171 with MF = 0

steps: data in the original packet = total size - header = 1600 - 30 = 1570
maximum data per fragment = MTU - header = 1400 - 30 = 1370
round down to a multiple of 8 -> 1368
total sizes add the 30-byte header back: 1398 and 232
offsets are in units of 8: 0 and 1368/8 = 171
chain.carry_forward: The whole of part 2 is one cascade from 1570 and 1368. A student who takes a wrong header or MTU loses the step where it goes wrong; the later fragment sizes, total sizes and offsets are then marked against their own earlier values, not against the scheme's.

questions.question: An organisation is granted a block of addresses with the beginning address 14.24.74.0/24. The organisation needs 5 sub-blocks: one of 10 addresses, one of 60, one of 120, one of 5 and the last of 6. Provide the block size, first valid host IP, last valid host IP and broadcast IP address for each sub-block.
questions.solution:
Each subnet must have at least (hosts + 2) addresses for network and broadcast, so take the next power of 2. Allocate with VLSM from 14.24.74.0, largest first, to avoid overlap.
Subnet 1 (120 hosts): block 128, /25. Network 14.24.74.0/25, range 0-127, first host 14.24.74.1, last host 14.24.74.126, broadcast 14.24.74.127.
Subnet 2 (60 hosts): block 64, /26. Network 14.24.74.128/26, range 128-191, first host 14.24.74.129, last host 14.24.74.190, broadcast 14.24.74.191.
Subnet 3 (10 hosts): block 16, /28. Network 14.24.74.192/28, range 192-207, first host 14.24.74.193, last host 14.24.74.206, broadcast 14.24.74.207.
Subnet 4 (6 hosts): block 8, /29. Network 14.24.74.208/29, range 208-215, first host 14.24.74.209, last host 14.24.74.214, broadcast 14.24.74.215.
Subnet 5 (5 hosts): block 8, /29. Network 14.24.74.216/29, range 216-223, first host 14.24.74.217, last host 14.24.74.222, broadcast 14.24.74.223.

rubric.point: Sub-block for 120 hosts: block size 128 (/25), network 14.24.74.0, first host 14.24.74.1, last host 14.24.74.126, broadcast 14.24.74.127
Sub-block for 60 hosts: block size 64 (/26), network 14.24.74.128, first host 14.24.74.129, last host 14.24.74.190, broadcast 14.24.74.191
Sub-block for 10 hosts: block size 16 (/28), network 14.24.74.192, first host 14.24.74.193, last host 14.24.74.206, broadcast 14.24.74.207
Sub-block for 6 hosts: block size 8 (/29), network 14.24.74.208, first host 14.24.74.209, last host 14.24.74.214, broadcast 14.24.74.215
Sub-block for 5 hosts: block size 8 (/29), network 14.24.74.216, first host 14.24.74.217, last host 14.24.74.222, broadcast 14.24.74.223

steps: each sub-block needs hosts + 2 addresses, rounded up to the next power of 2
allocate largest block first from 14.24.74.0 so the blocks do not overlap
each block's first host is network + 1, broadcast is the last address, last host is broadcast - 1
the next block starts immediately after the previous broadcast
chain.carry_forward: The five sub-blocks are one allocation running down the address space, so a wrong block size at subnet 1 shifts every later network address. Without carry-forward one early slip scores zero on all five items - ten marks lost for a single mistake. Mark each later sub-block against the student's own preceding boundary: award where the block size, the +1/-1 host edges and the broadcast are right relative to where they started.

questions.question: A large number of consecutive IP addresses are available starting at 10.198.16.0/16. Suppose that five organizations A, B, C, D and E request 10000, 8000, 6000, 4000 and 2000 addresses respectively, and in that order. Each network must include network + broadcast, so use the next power of 2 >= (needed + 2). A: 16,384 -> /18. B: 8,192 -> /19. C: 8,192 -> /19. D: 4,096 -> /20. E: 2,048 -> /21. Allocate sequentially from 10.198.16.0.

Organization B (8000 addresses): block 8192, network 10.198.80.0/19, first 10.198.80.1, last usable 10.198.111.254, broadcast 10.198.111.255
Organization C (6000 addresses): block 8192, network 10.198.112.0/19, first 10.198.112.1, last usable 10.198.143.254, broadcast 10.198.143.255

steps: block size = next power of 2 >= requested + 2
allocate sequentially from 10.198.16.0 in the order requested
first usable = network + 1; broadcast = last address of the block; last usable = broadcast - 1

questions.question: Consider the given weighted directed graph representing a network of routers. The numbers on the links represent link costs. Using Dijkstra's algorithm, find how the shortest path tree is constructed from the source node A to all other nodes. 1. Show the step-by-step execution of Dijkstra's algorithm (selection of next node, updating tentative distances, etc.). 2. Derive the final shortest path and total cost from A to each node. 3. Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm ensures optimality and termination.
questions.solution:
Initial: dist(A)=0, all others infinity, S = {}.
Step 0 - select A (dist 0). Update B: dist(B)=2, prev=A. Update C: dist(C)=5, prev=A. State: S={A}, dist={A:0, B:2, C:5, D:inf, E:inf}.
Step 1 - select B (dist 2). C candidate 2+3=5, no improvement (tie). D candidate 2+4=6 -> dist(D)=6, prev=B. E candidate 2+6=8 -> dist(E)=8, prev=B. State: S={A,B}, dist={A:0, B:2, C:5, D:6, E:8}.
Step 2 - select C (dist 5). E candidate 5+2=7, improves 8 -> dist(E)=7, prev(E)=C. State: S={A,B,C}, dist={A:0, B:2, C:5, D:6, E:7}.
Step 3 - select D (dist 6). E candidate 6+1=7, no improvement (tie). State: S={A,B,C,D}.
Step 4 - select E (dist 7). No updates. Final S={A,B,C,D,E}, algorithm terminates.
Final shortest paths from A: A->A cost 0; A->B cost 2 (A-B); A->C cost 5 (A-C, and A-B-C is also 5); A->D cost 6 (A-B-D); A->E cost 7 (A-C-E, or equally A-B-D-E).
Shortest path tree: prev(B)=A, prev(C)=A (or B), prev(D)=B, prev(E)=C (or via D). Tree edges: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-E.
Optimality: Dijkstra relies on the invariant that when it finalizes a node u with the smallest tentative distance d, no path from A to u can be shorter than d. This uses the assumption of non-negative edge weights; if negative edges exist the invariant breaks and Dijkstra can fail.
Termination: the algorithm finalizes one node per iteration and there are finitely many nodes (here 5), so after at most N selections all nodes are finalized and it stops.

rubric.point: Step-by-step execution: nodes are finalized in the order A, B, C, D, E, each time picking the smallest tentative distance and relaxing its neighbours
Final shortest distances and paths from A: B = 2 (A-B), C = 5 (A-C), D = 6 (A-B-D), E = 7 (A-C-E or A-B-D-E)

Optimality rests on the invariant that a finalized node's distance cannot be beaten, which needs non-negative edge weights; termination follows because one node is finalized per iteration and there are finitely many nodes

steps: repeatedly select the unfinalized node with the smallest tentative distance
relax each of its neighbours: candidate = dist(u) + cost(u,v)
final distances A:0 B:2 C:5 D:6 E:7
chain.carry_forward: The tentative distances at each step depend on every earlier relaxation, so one arithmetic slip propagates through the remaining steps. Mark the later steps against the student's own running distances: the credit is for applying the selection and relaxation rule correctly, not for reaching the scheme's numbers after an early error.

questions.question: Assume Network1, Network2 and Network3 with an IPv4 network and connectivity between these networks via the IPv6 internet, as shown in the figure. Mention the three strategies devised by the IETF to provide for a smooth transition from IPv4 to IPv6. Justify, with appropriate reasons, which strategy is more suitable if Network1 needs to communicate with Network3. Write the non-abbreviated form of the IPv6 addresses: A) FF02:30::5  B) 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329  C) 2000::1
questions.solution:
1. Dual Stack - devices run both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously; each interface has both addresses and can communicate using either protocol. Advantages: simple and flexible, no packet conversion needed. Disadvantages: requires all intermediate devices to support both, higher configuration and maintenance cost.
2. Tunneling - encapsulate IPv4 packets inside IPv6 packets (or vice versa) to cross an incompatible network; used when IPv4 islands must communicate across an IPv6-only core. Advantages: no need to upgrade the IPv6 core, allows IPv4 connectivity through an IPv6 backbone. Disadvantages: header overhead and processing complexity, may complicate MTU and fragmentation. Methods: 6to4, ISATAP, GRE over IPv6, manual tunnels.
3. Translation (NAT64 / DNS64) - convert IPv4 packets into IPv6 and vice versa at a translation gateway; used when IPv4-only and IPv6-only networks must interoperate. Advantages: enables communication when one side is IPv6-only. Disadvantages: breaks end-to-end transparency, applications embedding IP literals may fail.
Best suited strategy: Tunneling. Network1 and Network3 are IPv4-only and the core is IPv6; R1 encapsulates IPv4 packets inside IPv6 and sends them through the IPv6 internet, and R3 decapsulates and forwards them to Network3. No packet conversion or end-host modification is needed.
A) FF02:0030:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0005
B) 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329
C) 2000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
questions.breakdown_text: The marks column on this page is smudged on the scan. Part C is 20 and question 3 is printed as 5X2 = 10, which forces 10 here. The split - 2 per strategy, 1 for the justified choice, 1 per address - is ours.

rubric.point: Dual stack: devices run both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously, each interface carrying both addresses
Tunneling: IPv4 packets are encapsulated inside IPv6 packets to cross an incompatible network
Translation (NAT64 / DNS64): packets are converted between IPv4 and IPv6 at a translation gateway
Tunneling is the strategy best suited here, because Network1 and Network3 are IPv4 islands either side of an IPv6 core: R1 encapsulates and R3 decapsulates, leaving the end hosts unchanged
